overview: Obayashi Corporation (株式会社大林組), founded in 1892 and headquartered in Tokyo, is one of Japan's "Big 4"/"Big 5" sogo kensetsu (super general contractors) alongside Taisei, Shimizu and Kajima (and, unlisted, Takenaka). The group builds and engineers large-scale buildings and civil infrastructure in Japan and overseas (North America, Asia, Australia/UK via the 2026 Multiplex acquisition), and also develops and holds real estate, with a fiscal year ending March 31. Domestic construction is the core of the business (roughly 60% of consolidated net sales), supplemented by overseas construction (~33%), real estate development (~4%) and smaller green-energy/new-business initiatives.

business_model.summary: Obayashi earns the bulk of its revenue from fixed-price and cost-reimbursable construction contracts for buildings (offices, factories, data centers, hospitals, residential) and civil engineering works (roads, tunnels, dams, rail, disaster-resilience projects), recognized over the life of often multi-year projects. A smaller real estate development/leasing segment generates revenue from selling developed properties and rental income, and is a source of lumpy gains (e.g., FY ended March 2026 real estate operating profit nearly doubled on property sales). Revenue is overwhelmingly project-based and non-recurring rather than subscription-like; margins depend heavily on the vintage of backlog pricing versus current labor/material costs, so profitability lags and then overshoots the cost cycle as old low-margin contracts roll off and new, better-priced work is recognized.
business_model.customer_type: B2B/B2G — private developers, corporates and manufacturers (semiconductor fabs, data centers, logistics) for building construction; national/local government and utilities for civil engineering and disaster-resilience work; real estate development adds a smaller owned-asset/leasing and for-sale income stream
business_model.geographic_mix: Domestic Japan roughly two-thirds of consolidated net sales; overseas construction (North America, Asia, and now Australia/UK/Canada via Multiplex) around one-third and growing, aided by the GCON (US data center/semiconductor contractor, acquired FY2025) and Multiplex (announced June 2026) acquisitions

competitive_position.market_position: One of Japan's top-tier general contractors by revenue and technical capability, part of an oligopolistic group that dominates the largest, most technically demanding domestic projects (skyscrapers, long tunnels, dams, data centers, disaster-recovery work), while the broader Japanese construction market remains highly fragmented among thousands of smaller contractors

moat_factors.description: Over 130 years of experience on complex infrastructure and high-rise projects builds a qualification and trust advantage with large developers and government agencies that smaller contractors cannot easily replicate
Size and bonding capacity allow bidding on multi-year, multi-billion-yen projects beyond the reach of smaller rivals
Long-standing prequalified status on public infrastructure, resilience and disaster-recovery tenders provides recurring access to large public works
Limits the number of credible bidders for mega-projects, though competition among the five peers for major tenders remains real (and, historically, has tipped into illegal bid-rigging — see risks)

weaknesses: General contracting is fundamentally a thin-moat, highly competitive, labor-intensive business; Obayashi's own operating margin was only ~2% as recently as FY2022 (year ended March 2022)
Limited pricing power on legacy fixed-price contracts signed before recent cost inflation, which depressed margins for years until the backlog rolled over
No real product differentiation versus Taisei/Shimizu/Kajima/Takenaka on most tenders; price and schedule are often the deciding factors
History of regulatory/compliance risk — Obayashi was one of four Big-4 contractors found guilty of bid-rigging on the Linear Chuo Shinkansen maglev project in 2018
Heavy reliance on a shrinking, aging domestic skilled labor force, which increasingly constrains how much work the company can actually take on regardless of order demand

growth_drivers: Post-inflation backlog repricing: operating margin recovered from roughly 2% (FY2022) to 7.5% (fiscal year ended March 2026) as pre-2022 fixed-price contracts rolled off and newer, cost-reflective contracts were recognized

Japan's semiconductor/data center construction boom — TSMC/JASM-type fab ecosystem buildout plus hyperscale and urban data center demand; Obayashi's FY2025-acquired US subsidiary GCON specializes in semiconductor/data center construction, and the company launched its own urban data center venture, MiTASUN, targeting roughly ¥100 billion of investment with a first Tokyo facility slated for FY2028

June 2026 agreement to acquire Multiplex Global Limited from Brookfield (~$650 million including an earn-out) to accelerate expansion into Australia and the UK and strengthen its existing Canadian business — a rare large overseas M&A move for a Japanese contractor
Large-scale urban redevelopment in Tokyo/Osaka and infrastructure-renewal/disaster-resilience spending as Japan's postwar infrastructure ages
Growing overseas construction mix (North America, Asia) diversifying away from a demographically shrinking domestic new-build market

Continued share buybacks (¥58.1 billion in the fiscal year ended March 2026) and rising dividends (full-year dividend raised to ¥88, guided to ¥94 for the following year) as a capital-return lever alongside earnings growth

business.risk: Order backlog volatility and declining new orders
business.description: Consolidated orders received for the construction business fell 9.9% YoY (and non-consolidated orders fell 20.6% YoY) in the fiscal year ended March 2026 versus a prior year that benefited from large-project wins, illustrating the lumpiness of order intake and backlog
A portion of backlog can still reflect pre-inflation pricing; margin recovery depends on continued disciplined, profitability-focused bidding rather than chasing volume
Cross-border M&A (Australia/UK/Canada via Multiplex, US data centers via GCON) carries execution, cultural and regulatory-approval risk, and increases the company's overseas revenue and FX exposure

Obayashi, along with Taisei, Shimizu and Kajima, was found guilty by a Tokyo court in 2018 of rigging bids on sections of the Linear Chuo Shinkansen maglev project (2014-2015); recurrence or scrutiny of bidding practices on future mega-projects remains a tail risk given this history

financial.risk: Capital intensity of real estate and new ventures
financial.description: Real estate development, green energy, and data center investments (e.g., MiTASUN's ~¥100bn plan) require capital deployment with multi-year payback and some demand/price risk
Company is reducing cross-shareholdings toward a 20%-of-net-assets target by March 2027; pace and realized value depend on market conditions

regulatory.risk: Public infrastructure bidding rules and antitrust scrutiny
regulatory.description: Heavy reliance on government tenders exposes the company to procurement rule changes and renewed antitrust scrutiny, given the sector's history (maglev bid-rigging case) of coordinated bidding among the Big 4/5
Completion of the Brookfield/Multiplex deal (expected to close around Q4 2026) remains subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals in Australia, the UK and Canada

macro.risk: Skilled labor shortage and wage inflation
macro.description: Japan's construction workforce has shrunk from 6.85 million (1997) to 4.78 million (2025), with 36.6% of workers aged 55+ versus only 11.9% under 30; the April 2024 overtime cap ("2024 problem") constrains capacity further and construction-industry bankruptcies hit a 10-year high in 2025, with over 100 explicitly labor-shortage-driven failures

macro.risk: Raw material and construction cost inflation
macro.description: Steel, concrete, and equipment cost volatility remains a key swing factor on multi-year, partly fixed-price contracts
Rising BOJ rates raise financing costs for the company's balance sheet and could cool private building-construction/real estate demand

macro.risk: Cyclicality tied to capex and real estate cycles
macro.description: Order intake and margins are sensitive to corporate capital spending cycles (e.g., semiconductor/data center investment waves) and Japanese/global real estate investment sentiment
Overseas construction (~33% of sales) and recent acquisitions (GCON in the US, Multiplex in Australia/UK/Canada) increase translation and project-level FX exposure

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Japanese construction demand is shifting from new-build volume growth toward high-value, technically specialized work — semiconductor fabs, data centers, disaster-resilience/infrastructure renewal, and large urban redevelopment — a smaller but higher-margin pool than the historical new-build boom; near-term order environments for domestic building and civil engineering are described by management as firm, supported partly by reshoring of production and government-designated critical-product investment, even as some project cancellations/postponements occur
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high — multi-year order backlogs smooth revenue recognition but order intake, pricing and margins remain sensitive to corporate capex cycles, real estate investment sentiment and public infrastructure budgets
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — rising Japanese policy rates raise financing costs for the company and its real estate development arm, and could cool private construction demand; overseas (notably North American) rate moves also affect the overseas building/civil order environment
key_input_costs: Land/property acquisition costs for real estate development

recent_developments.event: Q1 FY2027 (April-June 2026) results: consolidated net sales ¥623.4bn (+19.0% YoY), consolidated operating profit ¥32.7bn (+107.0% YoY), profit attributable to owners of parent ¥39.0bn (+116.3% YoY), driven by property sales in real estate, completion of loss-provisioned projects, and highly profitable domestic building projects; consolidated orders received fell 7.2% YoY to ¥577.5bn against a strong prior-year comparison; full-year forecasts left unchanged from the May 13, 2026 guidance

Announced agreement (disclosed June 18, 2026) to acquire Multiplex Global Limited (the Wembley Stadium-building Australian/UK/Canadian contractor) from Brookfield for approximately $650 million (including an earn-out tied to future performance), aiming to accelerate expansion into Australia and the UK and strengthen its Canadian foundation; deal expected to close around Q4 2026 subject to regulatory approvals, with Multiplex's operations, projects, brand, and leadership (CEO John Flecker) expected to continue unchanged

Full fiscal year results for year ended March 31, 2026: consolidated net sales ¥2,586.3bn (-0.2% YoY), operating profit ¥194.7bn (+36.6% YoY, margin 7.5%), ordinary profit ¥204.2bn (+34.1%), profit attributable to owners of parent ¥173.8bn (+19.5%), ROE 14.4% (up from 12.6%); annual dividend raised to ¥88 (from ¥81), DOE ~5.1%; FY2027 (year ending March 2027) guidance set at net sales ¥2,945.0bn (+13.9%), operating profit ¥180.0bn (-7.5%), net income ¥157.0bn (-9.6%), citing a lower proportion of projects in final, most-profitable construction stages

Executed an up-to-¥40 billion share buyback program (completed, repurchasing ~15.14 million shares, 2.17% of shares outstanding) between August and December 2025, with shares subsequently cancelled; FY ended March 2026 total buybacks were ¥58.1bn versus ¥12.2bn the prior year

Acquired GCON, LLC and affiliated companies, a US contractor specializing in semiconductor/data-center construction, to build out overseas (North American) exposure to the AI/cloud-driven data center capex cycle

guidance.as_of: FY ended March 2026 results and FY2026 Q1 presentation (2026-05-13 / 2026-08-07)

items.notes: Growth driven by progress on a substantial volume of projects in hand in overseas building/civil engineering and continued domestic building strength; forecast reaffirmed unchanged as of the Q1 (Aug 2026) update

Expected decline reflects a lower proportion of projects in the final, most-profitable stage of construction in domestic building, limiting the benefit from additional claim approvals, change orders and cost reductions

items.metric: Profit attributable to owners of parent

items.notes: Expected to remain roughly flat as increases in domestic building and overseas civil engineering offset a decrease in overseas building orders versus the large-project-driven prior year
Both remain above the Medium-Term Business Plan 2022 targets of ROE ≥10% and ROIC ≥5%, and above WACC, despite the YoY decline

items.metric: Consolidated interest-bearing debt and nonrecourse loans
items.notes: Expected to decrease on continued collection of outstanding construction receivables following completion of large projects

items.vs_prior: raised from ¥88 the prior fiscal year
items.notes: Based on DOE policy of ~5%; FY ended March 2026 actual DOE was 5.1%, payout ratio 35.3%

guidance.management_commentary: Management attributes the FY ended March 2026 margin surge to a greater contribution from highly profitable construction projects, additional claim approvals and change orders in domestic building, steady progress in overseas civil engineering, and gains from real estate property sales. For FY ending March 2027, management explicitly flagged profit will decline even as sales grow, because fewer projects will be in the final, most-profitable stage of construction and the prior year benefited from one-off items (large claim approvals, property sales) that are not expected to repeat at the same scale.

bull_case: Multi-year margin recovery story: operating margin rose from roughly 2% (FY2022) to 7.5% (fiscal year ended March 2026) as the order backlog rolled over from pre-inflation to cost-reflective pricing, with ROE climbing from single digits to over 14%

Secular tailwinds from Japan's and North America's semiconductor/data center construction boom, reinforced by the GCON acquisition and the company's own MiTASUN urban data center venture, provide a technically demanding, less commoditized growth pool beyond traditional building/civil work

June 2026 Multiplex acquisition (Australia/UK/Canada) is a rare, meaningful overseas expansion for a Japanese contractor, diversifying revenue away from a shrinking domestic market and adding scale in markets with different demand drivers

Shareholder-friendly capital returns: dividend has been raised in successive years (¥81 to ¥88 to a guided ¥94) alongside an active buyback program (¥58.1bn in the fiscal year ended March 2026), supported by cross-shareholding unwind proceeds

Oligopolistic Big 4/5 market structure limits the number of credible competitors on Japan's largest, most complex redevelopment and infrastructure projects, and public infrastructure/resilience spending provides a steady floor of demand
bear_case: FY ending March 2027 guidance already signals declining operating profit and net income even as sales rise, reflecting the fading of one-off gains (claim approvals, property sales) and fewer projects in their most profitable completion stage — a reminder that the FY2026 margin surge may partly reflect a cyclical peak rather than a durable step-change

Japan's skilled-labor shortage is structural and worsening — the workforce has shrunk by roughly 30% since the 1990s, is heavily skewed toward workers 55+, and the 2024 overtime cap is constraining how much work contractors can physically execute, which can offset pricing gains with capacity limits and wage inflation

General contracting remains a fundamentally thin-moat, highly competitive, labor-intensive business; Obayashi has no meaningful product differentiation versus Taisei/Shimizu/Kajima/Takenaka and its historical margins (as low as ~2% in FY2022) show how quickly profitability can compress in a cost-inflation cycle

Order intake has already shown real volatility — consolidated construction orders fell 9.9% YoY and non-consolidated orders fell 20.6% YoY in the fiscal year ended March 2026 — illustrating how dependent recent results are on the timing of a handful of large projects

Regulatory/compliance tail risk is not purely historical: Obayashi was found guilty in 2018, alongside its three biggest domestic peers, of rigging bids on Japan's largest infrastructure project (the Linear Chuo Shinkansen maglev), underscoring the competitive intensity and governance risk inherent in bidding for Japan's largest public works

Cross-border acquisitions (GCON, Multiplex) add integration, FX and execution risk in markets (US data centers, Australia/UK/Canada construction) outside the company's traditional domestic competency, at a time when North American interest-rate direction for private real estate/data center capex is itself uncertain
